hook: The Siberian chemist who arranged the elements in the periodic table, and left gaps for new ones.

pages.x: Dmitri Mendeleev was born in 1834 near Tobolsk, in Siberia, the youngest of at least 14 children. His father, a teacher, went blind, and his mother ran a glass factory to keep the family going.

When the factory burned down, his mother took him, at 15, more than 2,000 km across Russia to find him a place at university, first in Moscow, then in St Petersburg. He got in, and she died soon after. He never forgot her.

A popular myth says he set the strength of Russian vodka at 40 per cent. He did not, though his doctoral thesis was about mixing alcohol and water. His real hobby was making suitcases, and he was proud of them.

Writing a textbook in 1869, he put each of the 63 known elements on a card, with its weight and properties, and laid them out like a game of patience. He saw that properties repeat in a regular pattern.
pages.fx: The periodic table organises all of chemistry, and hangs in every chemistry classroom in the world.

pages.x: He left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found yet, and described what they would be like.
pages.fx: Gallium, scandium and germanium were found within 17 years, just as he had said. The predictions convinced the world his table was a law of nature.

pages.x: In 1887 he went up alone in a hydrogen balloon to watch a total eclipse of the Sun from above the clouds, though he had never flown one before.
He narrowly missed the Nobel Prize in 1906, and died the next year. In 1955 a new element, number 101, was named mendelevium in his honour.
Mendeleev's periodic table brought order to the elements. It is the map of chemistry.
pts: Predicted elements that had not yet been found
Element 101, mendelevium, is named after him
